newsitem.title: GERMANY: Don't lag on euro preparations, EU warns Germany.
newsitem.headline: Don't lag on euro preparations, EU warns Germany.

text.p: With less than 700 days left to the launch of Europe's single currency, companies cannot afford to drag their heels on preparing for the switch to the euro, a top EU Commission official warned on Thursday.

At a conference in Frankfurt which saw German firms grappling with the tricky legal and technical problems the euro presents, Guiseppe Di Marco, an EU Commission administrator, said all companies, large or small, needed to take action.
"The next few months will give a clearer picture of how companies approach the switch. Competition will be the driving force," Di Marco said.

European law leaves firms free to adopt the euro as of January 1 1999, its planned launch date, or to wait until the start of 2002, when euro notes and coins come into circulation and national currencies cease to exist.
But for many large firms, the earlier they start using the euro, the better, Di Marco said.

"The launch of the euro will create an important new currency block which should offer additional liquidity compared with national currencies," he said. "Companies should at least consider using it as early as possible for financing."

Di Marco added that it was up to national governments, not the Commission, to create the legal structures companies need to convert their business to the euro. There were no plans for action on this at Commission level.
In Germany, a series of legal and practical hurdles have yet to be vaulted to prepare for the euro era, speakers and delegates at the conference said.

The euro switch, for instance, will cut the par value of the average German share from its current manageable level of five marks to a cumbersome 2.66 euros -- a value which violates German laws calling for rounded numbers for par values.

That presents a dillema for the more than 70 percent of Germany's top 100 companies which plan to convert their shares to euros during 1999, said Martin Bartels, a member of Dresdner Bank AG's syndicate team.

Possible solutions include a change in German law to allow irregular par values, or using a capital increase or decrease to create a more rounded base capital -- a costly operation which some companies will not be able to afford.

Finally, companies could adopt measures to remove currency par values from altogether, leaving their shares to represent a proportion of base capital -- the cheapest option and a system that is already common in Belgium and Luxembourg.
"In practice, we can probably live with a variety of solutions," Bartels said.

On a more positive notes, Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank AG board member Josef Wertschulte told the conference the euro presented German equity markets with their best chance yet of improving their global competitiveness.

With Germany likely to be regarded as a benchmark in the euro region, foreign investors were in future likely to opt to weight German equities far higher in a European portfolio than they do at present, Wertschulte said.
"The euro will be a key bridge for us in the next century, giving us access we never had before to the international capital we need," he said.
But the consensus among delegates was that Germany was facing a practical nightmare to try and get to grips with the euro.
"The real winners from the euro will be software companies ... and lawyers," said conference moderator Uwe Schneider.
"To be honest, we wouldn't mind a bit of a delay," a lawyer from a top German bank commented.
